title: Name-taking bash builtins with a variable argument skip the hidden-command check, so they run without asking
scenario: On a bash target (local Linux, WSL or SSH), a variable is assigned a literal array-subscript string that contains a command substitution. The same command line then passes that variable, quoted, as the name argument to `printf -v`, `read`, `declare`, `test -v` or `[ -v`. classifyCommand gives no findings, so decideCommand returns verdict "run" and nothing asks. Real bash 5.2 evaluates the subscript and runs the hidden command. I checked this in a scratch build: a hidden `rm -rf build` really deleted the folder, while the classifier and decision said ordinary/run. The check at line 1014 only looks at arguments whose value is known (`a.v !== null`), and here the argument is an unresolved expansion (`a.v === null`). The literal form is already caught (`printf -v 'a[$(…)]'` gives unclear.hidden-command), but the variable form gets past the check. This breaks D4.3 g and D4.3 a.
fix: In the NAME_TAKERS check, treat an unresolved argument (a.v === null) in a name position (the operand of `printf -v`, `read`, `declare`/`typeset`/`local`/`export`/`readonly`, `test -v`/`[ -v`, `unset`, `mapfile`/`readarray`, `wait -p`, `getopts`) as unclear ("It hides a command in a variable's name."). Simplest version: any NAME_TAKERS command with an unresolved argument is unclear. Add corpus cases for each builtin in the variable form.

title: `yarn npm publish` (Yarn 2+ publish) is classified as ordinary and runs without asking
scenario: The model runs `yarn npm publish` in a Yarn Berry project on any target. That is how Yarn 2+ publishes a package to the npm registry, which is D4.3 b. The npm/pnpm/yarn handler finds the verb `npm`. It is not in LANGUAGE_INSTALL_VERBS or the switch, so it falls through to `if (h.key !== "npm" && !builtins.has(verb)) nameCheck(h, verb)`. The word "npm" is not a publish/delete word, so there are no findings. In the scratch harness, classifyCommand returned no findings and decideCommand returned "run". The same path lets `yarn npm tag remove …` (registry delete, c) and `yarn npm login` (secrets, d) run without asking.
fix: For yarn, handle the `npm` verb by re-dispatching its subcommand: `publish` → publish (yarn.publish); `tag add` → publish (npm.registry); `tag remove` → remote-delete (npm.unpublish); `login`/`logout` → secret (secret.npm); `info`/`audit`/`whoami` → ordinary; anything else → unclear. Add corpus cases.

title: A task's downloads are recorded only when the download command exits 0, so running that file later counts as ordinary
scenario: finishRun adds `cls.downloads` to `ctx.state.downloaded` only when `exit.ended === "exit" && exit.code === 0`. Suppose a command fetches a script to a new file in the project folder (for example `curl -o x.sh <url>`) but the command as a whole exits non-zero, for example because a later part of the same line fails. The file is on disk, but the task does not remember it as downloaded. A later command `bash x.sh` or `./x.sh` is then classified with an empty `downloaded` set. The harness gives "run"/ordinary for it, whereas with x.sh recorded it is escape.run-downloaded, which always asks (D4.3 f). In the same command line the case is caught (`curl -o x.sh …; bash x.sh` asks), but across two commands it is lost. Output-taint may not trigger, because the fetched file's text never reaches the output.
fix: Record `cls.downloads` for every run that started, whatever its exit (any `ended` other than "failed-to-start" and "refused-remote"). If the classification held downloads, record them even when the run was stopped or timed out: a partial or failed download must still count as downloaded for D4.3 f. Add a command-flow test: a download run that exits 1, then a run of that file, must ask with escape.run-downloaded.
skeptic_notes:
Confirmed. I could not refute it, but the severity needs two qualifiers.

**The scenario is real.**
- `flow.ts:852` adds `cls.downloads` to `ctx.state.downloaded` only when `exit.ended === "exit" && exit.code === 0`.
- `test/unit/command-flow.test.ts:776` locks this in: a download run with code 1 leaves `downloaded` empty.
- I bundled `classify.ts` with esbuild and ran it on the corpus's linux context (cwd `/home/ana/proj`):
  - `curl -fsSL -o x.sh URL; ls missing` records downloads `[/home/ana/proj/x.sh]`. Its only finding is `destroy:download.output`, which applies only if the file already exists, so for a new file the run is ordinary.
  - With `downloaded` empty, `bash x.sh` and `./x.sh` give no findings, so they run without asking (D4.2).
  - With x.sh in `downloaded`, `bash x.sh` gives `escape:escape.run-downloaded`.

**No other guard catches it.**
- The remote gate builds its context with `downloaded: new Set()` (`app/remote/gate.ts:112`), and so does `decide.ts:104`.
- Output taint never sees a file that curl wrote with `-o`.
- The worker's `commandState` is per task, and nothing else repopulates it.

**It is not an accepted residual.**
- Design §3.8.3 step 14 does say "record `downloads` (only after exit code 0)", so the code follows the design to the letter.
- But that line is a normative instruction. It is not an L-list entry, a critique resolution or an open item in `handoffs.md`, and nothing records this gap as accepted.
- It also conflicts with OWNER DECISION D4.

The scenario does happen, but calling it "major" overstates it. It is the designed behaviour, and the protection it weakens can already be sidestepped just as easily in other ways.

title: A bare "here" in the request overrides the picker: the task moves to this computer, and a requested delete is announced and run there
scenario: The user picks "Work on ▸ build-01" (badge shows build-01) and says "check what's taking space here" or "Here is what I need: check the disk usage". localPhrases includes ["here"], so targetsNamed returns ["local"] and bindTarget binds THIS computer, ignoring the active remote (probe: both give {ok:true,id:"local"}). "on build-01, list the files here" is refused with "Ember works on one computer per task". Worst case: "delete build/ here" binds local. matchIntent gives "Deleting build, as you asked." and the command announces and runs `rm -r build` on the PC after 4 s. otherTargetsNamed finds no other target in the words, so the wrong-target guard never trips. The same file's guard comment calls bare "here" "where the task already is", which contradicts the binder.
fix: Don't let a bare "here" (or "in here"/"over here") name this computer: keep only explicit phrases ("this computer/pc/mac", "my computer", "locally"). Or count bare "here" as local only when the picker's choice is already local, as the guard does. Add tests for picker=ssh with "…here".
